desc:
prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i. You can make as many transactions as you like, where a transaction is one buy followed by one later sell. You may hold at most one share at any time, but you may sell and buy again on the same day.

Every transaction costs a fixed fee, paid once per completed buy-and-sell pair. Return the maximum total profit after fees. You are never forced to trade, so the answer is at least 0.

prices = [1, 3, 2, 8, 4, 9], fee = 2 -> 8
prices = [1, 3, 7, 5, 10, 3], fee = 3 -> 6

In the first example buy at 1 and sell at 8 (profit 7 - 2), then buy at 4 and sell at 9 (profit 5 - 2).
hints: Without a fee you would collect every rise. The fee makes tiny rises worthless and makes it costly to close and reopen a position.
At any time you are either holding a share or not. Track the best profit for each of the two states.
cash = max(cash, hold + price - fee) (sell today) and hold = max(hold, cash - price) (buy today). Update cash first, then hold, and return cash at the end.
editorial: Keep two numbers: cash, the best profit while holding nothing, and hold, the best profit while holding a share (the price already paid is subtracted). Starting values are cash = 0 and hold = -prices[0].

For each later price, selling today gives hold + price - fee and buying today gives cash - price. Take the better of 'do nothing' and 'act' for both states. Charging the fee at the sell is equivalent to charging it at the buy, as every sold share was bought exactly once.

The greedy view: a position is only closed when the price has dropped by more than the fee from the best level seen, which is exactly what the two-state update decides implicitly. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space.
solution:
def maxProfitWithFee(prices, fee):
    cash = 0
    hold = -prices[0]
    for x in prices[1:]:
        cash = max(cash, hold + x - fee)
        hold = max(hold, cash - x)
    return cash
